title: Containerd process loads one CPU core up to 100%
body: Recently I have twice seen containerd load one CPU core to 100% for a long time, like a busy loop. It can begin hours after containerd boots even though I have no containers running and no Docker images registered. I am using containerd v2.0.5 on Arch Linux x86_64 with kernel 6.14.5-arch1-1. The load stopped as soon as I attached gdb and exited; one thread was in epoll_wait and the others were in futexsleep. I shared the service log with a Go stack dump. When it happened again, I captured all thread backtraces and identified thread 8, LWP 37081, as the thread consuming the core, with its corresponding goroutine stack.

symptoms_visible: Containerd intermittently consumes one full CPU core for a long time even though I have no containers or images.
The spike can start hours after containerd boots and stops immediately when I attach gdb and exit.
N0.label: N0 intermittent idle CPU spike reported

symptoms_visible: When I run the ctr pprof command during a spike, containerd immediately becomes quiet before the profile can capture the sustained high-CPU behavior.
The spike seems more likely to begin while another unrelated process is also using substantial CPU.
N1.label: N1 pprof collection changes behavior

symptoms_visible: The spike has recurred after several profile attempts, and connecting through the debug socket or attaching strace still makes it stop immediately.
During one recurrence, strace showed repeated futex, non-blocking epoll_pwait, three-microsecond nanosleep, and eventfd write calls.
I later found dockerd consuming one full core with the same behavior while no containers were running.
N2.label: N2 repeated syscall evidence and dockerd recurrence

symptoms_visible: The same one-core spinning pattern is no longer limited to containerd on my machine: I have also observed it in dockerd.
Other affected systems running 6.14-series kernels show similar temporary full-core spikes in containerd and unrelated processes such as rclone, lxd, and gopls.
N3.label: N3 cross-process system-level pattern established

symptoms_visible: After installing kernel 6.14.9-arch1-1, I did not see containerd or dockerd peg a CPU core again during three days of monitoring.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved after kernel update

question_patterns: Can you enable the containerd debug socket and collect a CPU profile with ctr while the core is pegged?
Please run ctr pprof profile during the next recurrence and share the resulting profile.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I enabled the debug socket and ran `ctr --address=/run/containerd/debug.sock pprof profile > profile.log` as soon as I caught containerd loading a core. The process calmed down immediately when I ran the command, but I uploaded the resulting profile.log.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The profiling connection does not change the spike, and the captured profile consistently shows most CPU time in a containerd plugin function.
A second profile behaves the same way: the CPU drops as soon as I connect, and I upload another profile file.

question_patterns: Does the high CPU continue for the full profile collection, or does connecting to the debug socket affect it?
What happens to CPU usage at the moment ctr connects?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It stops spinning as soon as ctr connects to the debug socket, just like it does when I attach gdb or strace.

edges.comment: Original chain c1-c11, reporter's Arch system: pprof was requested as a measurement. The reporter supplied several raw profiles but repeatedly observed that the act of connecting stopped the spike, so profiling is not modeled as a fix.

question_patterns: Can you capture the busy thread with strace again during another recurrence and paste the raw syscall sequence?
If it happens again, what syscalls repeat immediately before the CPU drops?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: During another recurrence I attached strace to the busy thread. It printed repeated calls including `futex(..., FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE, 1)`, `epoll_pwait(..., 0, ...) = 0`, `nanosleep({tv_sec=0, tv_nsec=3000}, NULL) = 0`, more futex waits, and an eventfd `write(...) = 8`. Attaching strace again made the CPU usage drop.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The spike continues while strace is attached, and the trace consists almost entirely of repeated container filesystem reads with no epoll or futex activity.
The same syscall sequence appears, but the nanosleep interval is a few microseconds longer.

edges.comment: Original chain c12-c17, reporter's system: the repeated trace is raw measurement output. The reporter subsequently volunteered that busy-poll sysctls were zero and that dockerd later exhibited the same observable spin with no containers.

question_patterns: Does the same observable behavior occur in any other processes or on other affected systems?
What common environment details are present in the other reports of this full-core spin?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have now seen dockerd spin the same way on my machine with no containers running. Other affected users here report similar spikes in containerd and processes such as rclone, lxd, and gopls on 6.14.4 through 6.14.6 Arch or Arch-derived kernels. One user attached two CPU graphs from a 6.14.6-zen system.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I can reproduce it only in containerd, including on several older and newer operating-system environments where no other process exhibits the behavior.
The same cross-process pattern is reported on slightly different 6.14 patch releases.

edges.comment: Original chain c15-c20: participant4's Arch/Zen setup and screenshots, participant5's additional process reports, and the reporter's own dockerd observation are folded into one affected-user side. The reporter then volunteered a relevant upstream Linux commit link. The later 2026 Raspberry Pi log-view problem in c24-c28 is a distinct deployment and diagnostic chain and is intentionally excluded.

solution.intent: Treat the original incident as an operating-system kernel regression rather than a containerd defect: update to a kernel containing the upstream Linux fix, then monitor under normal and heavy activity for several days before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Upgrade the affected Arch system from kernel 6.14.5-arch1-1 to 6.14.9-arch1-1 or another build containing the upstream fix. Continue normal and heavy workloads and close the issue only if the one-core spikes do not recur; in the thread, the reporter observed no recurrence for three days.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw profiles, syscall traces, cross-process observations, affected system versions, and links to upstream Linux changes. Concluding that the original incident is a kernel regression fixed by the newer kernel is the diagnostic inference. The thread only links the upstream changes rather than explaining their implementation, so the answer should not invent a more specific kernel mechanism.

edges.comment: Resolution from c20-c23 on the original reporter's Arch system: the reporter installed 6.14.9-arch1-1 and observed no recurrence for three days, then attributed the issue to a Linux kernel bug fixed upstream. The reporter's own post-update observation supports terminal resolution.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause at the level established by the thread: an upstream Linux kernel regression, not a containerd-specific defect.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the spike occurred without container workload, profiling or debugger attachment changed the behavior, raw traces showed the repeating syscall activity, and similar spins appeared in dockerd and other processes on affected systems.
Must recommend moving to a kernel containing the upstream fix rather than proposing a containerd code or configuration change as the durable resolution.
Must not present gdb, strace, the debug socket, pprof collection, or a service restart as the permanent fix; those actions only stopped or disturbed an individual occurrence.
Must ask the reporter to monitor the updated system under normal or heavy activity for several days and must not declare resolution until the spike fails to recur.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced Linux user and systems troubleshooter: comfortable with systemd overrides, debug-symbol packages, gdb, strace, kernel configuration and sysctls, but unfamiliar with Go profiling tools and wants exact commands.
persona_hint.communication_style: Technical, precise, and cooperative. Shares raw traces and repeated measurements, clearly distinguishes observations from hypotheses, asks for concrete instructions, and waits for multi-day evidence before accepting a resolution.
